opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core problem is that once you've trained a model on something like the whole internet, it becomes really hard to know what you're actually measuring when you evaluate it. If I give a model a benchmark question and it gets it right, there are a lot of different stories you could tell about why. Maybe it really learned the underlying skill, the reasoning or the compositional generalization we care about. Or maybe some close variant of that exact question, or the benchmark itself, showed up somewhere in the training data, and the model is doing something closer to retrieval or pattern matching against things it's already seen.

With these huge pretraining corpora we usually can't fully audit what's in there, and even when we can, it's not obvious what counts as contamination. Is it the same problem with different numbers? The same structure with different surface words? At some point everything on the internet is a little bit related to everything else.

Synthetic data gives you a kind of control you don't otherwise have. You can construct tasks, or even little artificial languages or worlds, that you can be pretty confident the model has never encountered, and you can vary exactly the property you're interested in. Want to know whether a model can learn a new word from a couple of examples and use it compositionally? Invent the word. Want to know whether it can track the state of some system as it changes? Build a system whose rules don't exist anywhere else. Then success can't be explained by memorization, and failures become more interpretable too, because you know precisely what the model had to do.

It also lets you do something closer to real science, in the sense of controlled experiments. You can scale the difficulty, hold everything else fixed, and see where things break. That's very hard with naturally occurring data, where everything is confounded with everything else.

I don't think synthetic data is the whole story. There's always the risk that you build some toy task that's clean and interpretable but doesn't tell you much about how models behave on the messy things people actually use them for. So I see it as complementary: naturalistic evaluations tell you whether models are useful, and carefully constructed synthetic evaluations help you understand why, and which capabilities are actually there versus ones we're projecting onto them.

r001.rationale: The response says synthetic tasks can prevent benchmark contamination and make experiments controlled, but it does not explain that they avoid biases in natural data distributions that a model may have learned to exploit.

fable-5.1.text:
Jacob Andreas: Yeah, so I think the basic problem is one of contamination, broadly construed. When you have a model that's been trained on essentially the whole web, it becomes really hard to make claims about what the model is actually capable of versus what it's memorized or seen some very close variant of. If I want to ask, "Can this model do multi-step reasoning?" or "Can it acquire a new language from a grammar book?" or "Can it learn a new rule system from a few examples?", any natural benchmark I write down has some non-trivial chance of already being in the training data, or of having a near-duplicate in there. And it's not just literal test set leakage. There's this softer version where the specific task format, the specific kinds of problems, the solutions to structurally similar problems are all over the internet, and so you're measuring retrieval dressed up as reasoning.

Synthetic data lets you sidestep that. If I construct a formal language with a grammar I made up last week, or a planning domain with rules that don't exist anywhere, then I know for sure the model hasn't seen it. So whatever performance I observe has to be coming from some general capability, some ability to pick up structure from the context or from a small amount of fine-tuning data, rather than from recall. That's really the only way I know of to get a clean answer to the question of what the model can do in principle.

There's a second reason that I think is underappreciated, which is control. With synthetic data you get to vary things systematically. You can hold everything fixed and change one dimension of difficulty: the depth of a derivation, the number of entities you have to track, the length of a dependency. Natural data is incredibly confounded. Hard problems in the real world tend to be hard for lots of reasons at once, so when a model fails, you don't learn much about why. With a synthetic task you can actually draw the curve and say the model handles this up to depth four and then falls apart, and that's a much more informative scientific statement.

Now, the obvious criticism is that synthetic tasks are artificial, and if the model does poorly on my made-up grammar, who cares? And I think that's partly right. I don't think synthetic evaluations tell you whether a model is useful. What they tell you is something about the mechanisms, about the kinds of generalization the model can and can't do. And so the way I think about it is that the two things are complementary. Real-world benchmarks tell you how the model does on the distribution people actually care about, and synthetic ones let you understand what's going on underneath, in a setting where you have some hope of actually controlling the variables.

r001.rationale: The response says internet-pretrained models may have seen natural benchmarks or similar task formats and solutions, making evaluation measure retrieval rather than reasoning. It explains that synthetic tasks with novel rules can avoid this influence.

astra-6.text:
I think the fundamental challenge is that if you take an existing benchmark, or even write down a question whose answer is somewhere on the internet, it’s very hard to know whether the model is solving the problem or remembering something it saw during training. Those can look exactly the same from the outside.

Synthetic data gives us a little more control over that distinction. We can construct a new little world, specify the rules of that world, and ask the model to reason about them. We can also vary individual aspects of the problem: how many steps you need to solve it, which combinations of things you’ve seen before, or how much irrelevant information is present. That lets us ask more precise questions about what the model can do and where it breaks down.

Of course, being good at a synthetic task doesn’t automatically mean you can handle the corresponding real-world task. But if we want to understand what these models have learned, rather than just measure how well they perform on familiar questions, having that kind of experimental control is really valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says synthetic tasks help distinguish reasoning from memorization and allow controlled variation, but it does not explain that they avoid biases in natural data distributions that a model may exploit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic challenge is that if you want to understand what a model can do, you need some way of separating what it learned to do from what it might have seen before. If you take a question from an existing benchmark, or even write a question about some well-known fact, it’s hard to know whether the model is solving the problem or reproducing something from its training data.

Synthetic data gives us a little more control. We can invent a small world, specify the rules of that world, and then ask the model questions whose answers follow from those rules. We can vary the number of reasoning steps, or hold out particular combinations of things, and see where it succeeds and where it breaks down.

Of course, being synthetic doesn’t automatically make a dataset a good evaluation. You can accidentally introduce shortcuts, and success in a toy world doesn’t necessarily tell you how a model will behave in the real world. But it gives you a way to test a specific hypothesis about what the model has learned, which is much harder when you don’t know exactly what it has already encountered.

r001.rationale: The response says synthetic worlds can control the rules and reveal shortcuts, but it does not explain that synthetic evaluation can avoid biases in natural data distributions that an internet-pretrained model may exploit.
